doc.title: Tommy Newsom and Ross Tompkins interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Marijuana Reeds dates; decline of studio and Broadway work
summary: Ross recalls the Marijuana Reeds with Zoot Sims; synthesizers and overdubbing reduced demand, and pit bands shrink.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Studio work and jingles: New York session life

blocks.x: There was some fine record dates. Do you remember the “Marijuana Reeds” with Zoot Sims and Gene Quill.
Yeah, so instead of the Tijuana Brass they called them the Marijuana Reeds.
A group that Al Cohn named, it was Gene Quill and Phil Woods, he called them Leopold and Loeb.
People will have to work that out.

Well starting out, I mean years ago, there was a lot of work and they used a lot of people. It was like a large amount of work and a large workforce. And in L.A. too. In fact, New York was busier than L.A. at the time I’m talking about, in the late 50s. And then when the machines came in, like synthesizers, and improvement in tape techniques, you know where they could overdub things and sel-sync things, you know? Well you’d make strings sound like twice as many people while they’re playing. All of that diminished the demand. And it’s sad to say it’s dwindling down. And New York is mainly Broadway now.

Yeah, and even the Broadway, I’m not sure how it is there, but when we see some of the shows that come up in Central, New York, the pit bands are six and seven people. And they always have two or three people on a keyboard.
And you’re hearing all these things that are—
Yeah, I don’t know in the city I doubt they’re doing that but I don’t know. Who do I know that does that. I know Bill Crow and Joe Wilder, they’re still Broadway.
